task: Write one sentence of your own using the word rebuke. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know rebuke should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The archivist rebuked the visiting researcher in front of the whole reading room for uncapping a pen above the folios.
To correct someone fixes the error and moves on; a rebuke makes sure the error's owner feels its weight.
Lambaste goes past rebuke: the rebuked pilot gets thirty stinging seconds, while the lambasted one gets the full verbal thrashing, at length and in front of witnesses.

Scold is the everyday, kitchen-table word for angry correction — a parent over a broken curfew, a roommate over the dishes. A rebuke is a scolding with rank behind it: sharp, formal, and delivered downward by someone with the standing to correct you. Anyone can scold; a rebuke comes from authority.

A reprimand is the official version of a scolding — written up and kept in the file, in the measured language of an institution. A rebuke is hotter and more immediate: delivered to your face, in the moment, and done. The reprimand outlives the meeting; the rebuke ends with it.

Old French buker ('to strike') died out on both sides of the Channel; rebuke is the only English word it left behind. Hear the fossil anyway — a rebuke still lands like the blow the word was built from.
Rebuke means to scold sharply.

The flight instructor let the landing finish before she spoke, and then she rebuked him and did not soften it: skipping the crosswind checklist, she told him, was how licenses ended and how worse things began, and he would fly the pattern again until the checklist was reflex.
Ten words of it carried into the next hangar.
It stung — it was meant to.
Rebuke is the exact word because the scolding is sharp, direct, and delivered downward — an authority correcting a fault to its face.
To reproach him would be gentler, more sorrow than sting; a lecture would take an hour.
A rebuke is short, hot, and lands like a slap of cold water.
Rebuke is the sharp, face-to-face scolding an authority delivers in the moment — judges rebuke attorneys, harbormasters rebuke captains.
Its unit-mate reproach is the soft-spoken cousin: more disappointment than heat, often between equals or loved ones.
If the scolding comes stamped and filed, reprimand is the bureaucrat's word for the same sting.

The head chef ran her kitchen on two rules — taste everything, waste nothing — and everyone from dishwasher to sous-chef knew both by the end of day one.
When the new sauté cook tipped a pan of scorched garlic into the stock instead of starting over, she crossed the kitchen in four strides.
The rebuke lasted fifteen seconds, was delivered an inch from his ear, and carried over every burner in the room.
She tasted the repaired stock an hour later, nodded once, and never mentioned the garlic again.
Cooks who trained under her say the sting faded fast, but nobody ever ruined a stock twice.
